draft_quotes: The dispute arises from Civil Appeals Nos. 189 and 190 of 1952, heard in the civil appellate jurisdiction on December 14, 1953 [S6fd756c20d26][S1013eb0fed1a]. The plaintiff, Kalyanpur Lime Works Ltd. (the Lime Co.), instituted a suit for specific performance of a contract with the State of Bihar (Defendant No. 1), impleading Dalmia Jain & Co. Ltd. as Defendant No. 2 [S8e11b47725c3]. The primary relief sought was specific performance of the alleged lease contracts, possession, and compensation, following Defendant No. 1's refusal to execute leases and its decision to lease the property to Defendant No. 2 on June 2, 1949 [S106d60d4a58a].

The subject matter is the Murli Hills in Shahabad District. On April 1, 1928, Defendant No. 1 leased the hills to Kuchwar Lime and Stone Co. (Kuchwar Co.) for 20 years for quarrying limestone [S830e8b76ae83]. The lease prohibited assignment without Government permission [S861302b02ec6]. In January 1933, Kuchwar Co. went into voluntary liquidation, and its liquidators purported to assign the leasehold interest to Subodh Gopal Bose for Rs. 35,000 via an unregistered deed dated September 30, 1933 [S861302b02ec6][S49406c28d920]. The assignee took possession but was stopped by Government orders in December 1933 due to breach of the assignment prohibition [S49406c28d920].

The Lime Co. applied for the lease on January 25, 1934, offering a minimum royalty of Rs. 10,000 [Sa9e8aaafd99d]. On March 27, 1934, Defendant No. 1 forfeited the Kuchwar Co. lease and re-entered possession [Sa7d4a6c96918]. Thereafter, Defendant No. 1 offered to grant leases to the Lime Co. for 20 years on terms set forth in Chapter V of the Bihar & Orissa Waste Lands & Mineral Concession Manual [S2c4036b2445a]. This offer (Annexure B) was accepted by the Lime Co. (Annexure C) on April 15, 1934, and the Lime Co. obtained possession effective April 1, 1934 [S2c4036b2445a].

Kuchwar Co. sued the Secretary of State for India in September 1934, challenging the forfeiture. While the trial court dismissed this suit, the High Court of Patna decreed it on February 7, 1936, affirming that the leases had not been validly forfeited [Sd6c529f926cc]. An ad interim injunction issued in April 1935 restrained the Government from granting leases to the Lime Co. [Sc0a06713e0fd]. Although the Lime Co. was not a party to the Kuchwar suit, it continued in possession until April 1936, when it vacated the quarries after contempt proceedings against its managers were initiated by Kuchwar Co. [S6e36386cb99b]. The Privy Council affirmed the High Court’s decision favoring Kuchwar Co. in November 1937 and set aside the contempt order in October 1938, but the Lime Co. did not succeed in getting restitution [Sc0a06713e0fd][S6e36386cb99b]. Kuchwar Co. surrendered possession when its lease expired on March 31, 1948, at which point Defendant No. 1 re-entered possession [S75fed3609fe9].

The primary relief sought was specific performance of the alleged lease contracts, possession, and compensation, following Defendant No. 1's refusal to execute leases and its decision to lease the property to Defendant No. 2 on June 2, 1949 [S106d60d4a58a].
Defendant No. 1 resisted the suit, arguing no concluded contract existed, that negotiations fell through, and raising pleas of limitation, estoppel, acquiescence, and waiver [S9d91cc92c6cb].

Defendant No. 2 denied the Lime Co.’s legal existence and right to sue, claimed the Government’s actions were based on misapprehension, and asserted protection as a subsequent lessee for valuable consideration without notice of any binding equity [Sbb7de2829ba0][S575f63eec68a].

The trial court framed issues regarding the existence of a valid contract and whether essential terms were settled [S958afad0b839][S80dc026f442c]. It found that the correspondence between the Lime Co. and the Board of Revenue constituted a valid agreement for a 20-year lease commencing from execution, with royalties distributed as Rs. 7,500 for the upper hill and Rs. 2,500 for the lower hill [S06cd204b2cf0][Sa9049bcb69cf]. The trial court rejected defenses of lack of legal existence, limitation, estoppel, waiver, and acquiescence [Sbeb571c7196c]. It held that Defendant No. 2, having notice of the prior contract, lacked locus standi to contest specific performance [Sbeb571c7196c]. Consequently, the trial court decreed specific performance and compensation from April 1, 1948, leaving the amount of compensation to be determined later [S97682527e61d].

The High Court reversed the decree, dismissing the suit [Se1ce994deacd]. While agreeing that a contract was made, the High Court held the specific contract pleaded was void under Section 20 of the Indian Contract Act due to mutual mistake of fact regarding the Government’s title [S4da221281e65]. It also deemed the agreement void under Section 30 of the Government of India Act, 1915, for non-compliance with statutory conditions [S4da221281e65]. The High Court refused relief under Section 18(a) of the Specific Relief Act, viewing it as reconstruction of the agreement, and denied alternative relief under Section 15 because the Lime Co. had not relinquished all further claims [S4da221281e65][S06087d490791]. It further found the Lime Co. was not ready and willing to perform, was not the real plaintiff, and that discretion should not be exercised in its favor [S06087d490791].

A significant procedural objection concerns the issue of "mutual mistake." The trial court initially framed a draft issue on this ground but deleted it on November 29, 1950, upon the plaintiff’s objection [Sa23514d45d95][Sc8d351d04916]. Counsel for the defendants conceded they did not challenge the contract’s validity on grounds of mistake of fact or law, nor was such an allegation in their written statements [S651702051afd]. This concession contradicts the High Court’s reliance on mutual mistake.

The High Court disallowed the claim under Section 15 of the Specific Relief Act, finding the plaintiff’s application dated February 18, 1952, did not sufficiently relinquish claims for past deficiency or damages [S952f65c826eb]. However, the plaintiff’s counsel orally clarified during arguments that they insisted on no further performance and claimed no compensation for periods prior to the execution of leases [Sed355cb02b6e]. The written application alternatively claimed specific performance for the period after April 1, 1949, while relinquishing claims for periods prior to April 1, 1948 [S2fb2a70d0810][S7093796118f1].

Regarding evidence, the Lime Co. sent six copies of draft leases to Defendant No. 1 [S4538bb57e9b7]. Despite multiple applications and court orders directing production, Defendant No. 1 failed to produce these documents [S0f896b0e1c26][S561ba2462cc0][Sed979d2f7f61].

unresolved: The Supreme Court's final reasoning on whether the High Court erred in applying Section 20 ICA given the trial court's issue framing.
Whether the Lime Co.'s oral clarification of relinquishment satisfied Section 15 SRA requirements in the eyes of the apex court.
The precise legal effect of the Privy Council's contempt ruling on the Lime Co.'s standing to claim restitution or specific performance.
